content: 1. Following treatment, 18 out of 21 participants in the intervention group reported experiencing slight but noticeable change, while 10 out of 21 reported definite improvement. These findings suggest a favorable response to the intervention. 2. No studies were available to assess the impression of change during follow-up periods, nor were there studies evaluating fatigue outcomes post-treatment or during follow-up. 3. The outcomes of fatigue and impression of change were considered important, while all other outcomes were deemed critical for evaluation. 4. Effect sizes were reported as standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals unless otherwise specified. 5. Psychological interventions, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), behavioral therapy (BT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and relaxation training (RT), were compared to standard care, wait-listed controls, or active non-psychological interventions. Additional stratified analyses are detailed in Web Annexes F and G. 6. Seven studies involving 702 participants reported no treatment-related adverse events (AEs) in any trial arm. One study noted more AEs in the control arm (education + amitriptyline) compared to the treatment arm, with most AEs attributed to amitriptyline. 7. Post-treatment and follow-up data on fatigue were not available in the reviewed studies. 8. Patient satisfaction with treatment was assessed in three studies involving 695 participants. One study found that a higher percentage of participants treated with sumatriptan and naproxen reported being satisfied or very satisfied with the medication's overall effectiveness and their overall satisfaction at 2 and 24 hours post-dose (unadjusted P ≤ 0.014). 9. The certainty of evidence was assessed for all combined studies but not for subgroups involving CBT, ACT, BT, and RT. 10. Among children aged 9 years and older, psychological interventions were found to improve sleep problems, anxiety, mood, and quality of life. These skills were perceived as transferable to daily life. 11. Children aged 9 years and older reported that psychological interventions alleviated pain levels for conditions such as neck pain, abdominal pain, lupus, and headaches/migraines. 12. Group-based psychological and physical interventions normalized chronic pain experiences for children and facilitated sharing of experiences, which was perceived as supportive. However, some children felt guilt or discomfort in group settings if they perceived their pain as less severe than others. 13. Families often found it burdensome to travel for repeated face-to-face intervention sessions, which posed a barrier to participation in both physical therapy (PT) and psychological interventions. 14. Social support, such as assistance from school staff, improved adherence to PT interventions. Parents also expressed a need for ongoing social and booster support after the intervention programs ended. 15. The time required to complete prescribed exercise programs was challenging to fit into children’s existing school, homework, and social commitments. Exercises integrated into school time or those requiring less than 30 minutes were more likely to be adhered to. 16. Parents of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) recommended peer-accepted lifestyle activities of less than 30 minutes, mechanisms to track improvements, and adaptations of exercises based on the child’s current health status to maintain engagement in home exercise programs. 17. Some healthcare providers (HCPs) expressed concerns about opioid addiction in children, leading to untreated pain. This fear was particularly noted in Thailand and Morocco. 18. In contrast, parents of children with cancer in Jordan, Cameroon, and Indonesia expressed acceptance of opioid treatment for pain management, including palliative care. Free provision of oral morphine in rural communities was welcomed. 19. Cultural beliefs sometimes acted as barriers to pain management. For example, in Morocco, some families viewed pain as inevitable and something to be endured, particularly by boys. In Zambia, traditional beliefs attributing illness to witchcraft hindered cooperation with pain management strategies. 20. In some cultures, children may not openly express their pain. HCPs need to consider children’s values and beliefs to improve the quality of pain management and care.
